clue.text: Trollope's Solicitor-General recalls Wycherley's 19 priest

definitions.meaning: Sir Timothy ... is the ambitious Solicitor-General in Trollope's novel The Three Clerks
in Wycherley's play The Country Wife a gallant of this name disguises himself as a clergyman, so he is a phony priest (19-across gives PHONY)

explanation.walkthrough: The '19' points to the answer at 19-across, PHONY: the Wycherley character is a sham priest. 'recalls' just links the two literary definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: Two characters share the surname: one Trollope's law officer, the other a disguised suitor in a Restoration comedy.

clue.text: A large drink, say, for David's wife

indicators.note: say signals that the phrase before it is spoken and heard, not spelt

parts.note: a big ale, a large glass of beer

explanation.surface: Someone orders a large drink, perhaps, on behalf of David's wife.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Bible Abigail became one of King David's wives after the death of her husband Nabal.

clue.text: Some incisive writing from the Middle East

definitions.text: Some incisive writing from the Middle East

parts.words: Some incisive writing from the Middle East
parts.note: incisive sounds like sharp prose, but the writing is literally cut into clay with a wedge-shaped stylus in ancient Mesopotamia

explanation.definitionFit: The ancient wedge-shaped script of Sumer and Babylon was pressed or incised into clay tablets.

clue.text: Loss of content in wonderful Lagerkvist novel

indicators.note: in tells us the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Something is missing from a marvellous novel by the Swedish writer Pär Lagerkvist.
explanation.definitionFit: Ullage is the amount by which a cask or bottle falls short of full, the contents lost by leakage or evaporation.

clue.text: Maskwell

parts.note: Maskwell is the scheming villain of Congreve's comedy, and his name read as 'mask well' describes a two-faced schemer

explanation.definitionFit: Congreve's 1693 comedy centres on Maskwell, a treacherous schemer who betrays everyone while pretending friendship.

clue.text: Masters described its nocturnal athletes?

parts.note: John Masters wrote the novel Night Runners of..., and the runners of the night are playfully called athletes

explanation.definitionFit: John Masters's 1951 novel of the Indian Mutiny is titled Night Runners of Bengal, after a region of eastern India.

clue.text: Well-known collaborator, crazy about men

indicators.note: crazy means wildly disordered, so the letters of the two words after it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A famous partner is said to be mad about men.
explanation.walkthrough: Francis Beaumont wrote plays jointly with John Fletcher, the best-known partnership of Jacobean drama.
explanation.definitionFit: The Jacobean dramatist worked in a famous writing partnership with John Fletcher.

clue.text: Coarse character in early German satires offers complaint about British Isles

definitions.text: Coarse character in early German satires

indicators.note: about here means surrounding, so one piece wraps round the other

parts.note: a groan is a complaint
BI is the abbreviation for British Isles

explanation.surface: A boorish figure from old German satire grumbles about Britain and Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Grobianus was the boorish anti-hero of sixteenth-century German satire, giving a name for any lout or clown.

clue.text: Modern like some of Carlyle's pamphlets

definitions.meaning: Thomas Carlyle published his ... Pamphlets in 1850

explanation.definitionFit: The compound means belonging to recent times, and Carlyle used it to title his 1850 pamphlets on contemporary society.

clue.text: Lenten cake for 19 king

definitions.meaning: a rich fruit cake topped with marzipan, eaten in Lent and at Easter
19-across gives PHONY: Lambert ... was a pretender crowned in Dublin as Edward VI in 1487

explanation.definitionFit: The fruit cake of mid-Lent shares its name with Lambert Simnel, a sham claimant to Henry VII's throne.

clue.text: Friend of Uncle Tom with game fish in Bowen book

parts.note: little Eva is Tom's young friend in Uncle Tom's Cabin
the trout is a game fish

explanation.surface: A companion of Uncle Tom turns up with a fish in a novel by Elizabeth Bowen.
explanation.definitionFit: Elizabeth Bowen's last novel, from 1968, is named after its awkward heiress heroine.

clue.text: Paul Goodman improvising

definitions.meaning: the American writer Paul Goodman published a novel of this title in 1963
managing with whatever is to hand

explanation.definitionFit: Getting by with what is available is improvising; Paul Goodman also used the phrase as a novel title.

clue.text: Margaret Halsey bore it towards some

definitions.text: Margaret Halsey bore it towards some

parts.words: Margaret Halsey bore it towards some
parts.note: Margaret Halsey's 1938 travel book is With ... Toward Some, echoing Lincoln's 'with ... toward none'

explanation.definitionFit: Halsey's witty book on England is titled With Malice Toward Some, so she bore ill will towards some.

clue.text: Kent warship

parts.note: Kent is not the county but Alexander Kent, the naval novelist who wrote ... of War about a small warship

explanation.definitionFit: A small single-masted warship is one; Alexander Kent's Bolitho novel is titled Sloop of War.

clue.text: Plunder French town for English poet

parts.note: to sack a city is to plunder it
ville is French for town

explanation.surface: Raiders loot a French town to provide for an English poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Sackville co-wrote Gorboduc and contributed to A Mirror for Magistrates; Vita Sackville-West also descends from the family.

clue.text: Condon's woman, deserted, or dissolute?

definitions.meaning: Richard Condon wrote the novel The ... Woman (1977)
wildly unrestrained, given over to vice

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both forsaken and wholly unrestrained in behaviour, and Richard Condon used it in a novel title.

clue.text: Buck Book expressly a no-no in Exodus,

definitions.meaning: the first commandment in Exodus forbids worshipping any rivals to the Lord

explanation.definitionFit: Exodus 20 commands 'Thou shalt have no other gods before me', and Pearl Buck took the phrase as a title.

clue.text: "It was more like an in a farce of Moliere's" (Stevenson)

definitions.text: "It was more like an in a farce of Moliere's" (Stevenson)

parts.words: "It was more like an in a farce of Moliere's" (Stevenson)
parts.note: the missing word from Stevenson's sentence is a French term for an interlude between acts of a play

explanation.definitionFit: An interlude performed between the acts of a play, here something comic in a Moliere farce.

clue.text: Associated with academic by Patrick O'Brian?

definitions.text: Associated with academic by Patrick O'Brian?

parts.words: Associated with academic by Patrick O'Brian?
parts.note: an academic is a Master (of Arts), and O'Brian's first Aubrey novel joins a Master with this naval rank

explanation.definitionFit: Patrick O'Brian's novel Master and Commander pairs the word with master, a term also for an academic graduate.

clue.text: Somehow impanel a Roman infantry unit

indicators.note: somehow suggests the letters of the next word are put together in some other way

explanation.surface: A Roman army unit is somehow sworn in as a jury.
explanation.definitionFit: The maniple was a subdivision of the Roman legion, about 120 to 200 soldiers.

clue.text: Daladier's sort of war

parts.note: Edouard Daladier was French premier during the inactive first months of the Second World War, the drole de guerre

explanation.definitionFit: The quiet months from September 1939 to spring 1940 were nicknamed the sham or bogus war.

clue.text: "At last, fortissimo!", Mahler said, on visiting it

definitions.text: "At last, fortissimo!", Mahler said, on visiting it

parts.words: "At last, fortissimo!", Mahler said, on visiting it
parts.note: Mahler is said to have exclaimed 'Endlich ein Fortissimo!' on seeing the great falls on the US-Canada border

explanation.definitionFit: The thundering falls between New York State and Ontario drew Mahler's famous remark about real loudness.

clue.text: Some caper cut by French writer, showing insight

indicators.note: some means only part of the words that follow is used

explanation.surface: A bit of a lark is trimmed by a French author, which shows real perception.
explanation.definitionFit: An apercu is a brief illuminating glimpse or perception, a flash of understanding.

clue.text: Material for cover-up introduced by Dickens's Anastasia, who …

indicators.note: introduced by means only the opening part of the name is used, the tail dropped

parts.note: Anastasia Veneering is the social-climbing wife in Dickens's Our Mutual Friend

explanation.surface: A Dickens hostess brings in material to hide something, leading into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs the clue into 23-across; dropping ING from VENEERING leaves the start of her surname.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin layer of fine wood glued over cheaper timber is a covering material.

clue.text: … may preen absurdly. Heavens above!

indicators.note: absurdly means in a ridiculous arrangement, so the letters of may preen are jumbled

explanation.surface: Anastasia Veneering may primp herself ridiculously, prompting an exclamation of dismay.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest heaven, the realm of pure fire in ancient cosmology, lies above everything.

clue.text: "On the — / I thrice presented him a kingly crown" (Julius Caesar)

definitions.text: "On the — / I thrice presented him a kingly crown" (Julius Caesar)

parts.words: "On the — / I thrice presented him a kingly crown" (Julius Caesar)
parts.note: Mark Antony's funeral speech recalls offering Caesar the crown at the Roman festival held in February

explanation.definitionFit: The Lupercalia was the Roman fertility feast at which Antony offered Caesar a crown.

clue.text: Agreement in railway article for Japanese stop over

indicators.note: in signals that one piece is placed inside the others

parts.note: an is the indefinite article
OK expresses agreement

explanation.surface: A deal is struck inside a railway feature about an overnight stay in Japan.
explanation.definitionFit: A traditional Japanese inn where travellers stay the night.

clue.text: Come out, like Arnold's new-bathed stars

definitions.meaning: Matthew Arnold's poem Self-Dependence describes the stars that 'new-bathed' come out into view

explanation.definitionFit: Coming into view is the action, and Arnold applies the verb to stars rising freshly washed from the sea.

clue.text: Customs man recognized as primitive

parts.note: Henri ..., nicknamed Le Douanier because he worked as a customs official, became famous as a naive painter

explanation.definitionFit: The French painter Henri Rousseau, a toll collector by trade, is the classic primitive or naive artist.
